profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting at a mid-sized investment bank to evaluate a proposal for updating the internal market risk methodology used in the Treasury risk dashboard. The proposal is based on a comparative report showing that Filtered Historical Simulation (FHS) outperforms Historical Simulation and GARCH-Normal for daily 5% VaR and multi-day tail-risk estimation. The meeting's agenda is to review whether the proposed FHS design package is ready to be taken to the bank's Model Methodology Committee, confirm what will be shown in the pilot rollout, and identify any gaps before approval. The expected outcome is apparent agreement to move forward with the committee submission and a Treasury pilot, without either participant realizing they are using different assumptions about what exactly is being reviewed and deployed.

members.name: Elena Rossi
members.expertise: VaR modeling, volatility modeling, backtesting, quantitative validation
members.background: Elena is a former sell-side quant with a PhD in financial econometrics who now leads methodology changes for the bank's market risk models.
members.private_state: She wants the FHS proposal through committee this cycle so the bank can close a long-running remediation item on VaR performance, and she is quietly trying to avoid expanding the review into reporting and controls work that would delay approval.
hidden_assumptions: When colleagues say 'the 5-day backtest,' they mean the overlapping 5-day forecast evaluation used in the methodology study unless they explicitly ask for a governance-only format.
A 'Treasury pilot' naturally means the subset of rates and FX books already supported by the quant infrastructure, not every position shown in the broader Treasury dashboard.
Using the 'same data cut' means using the 6 p.m. New York risk snapshot aligned with the return series in the model study, because that is the proper methodological basis.
If a design is 'ready for committee,' the required threshold is methodological completeness and validation evidence; implementation notes and desk instructions can follow after conceptual approval.

members.name: Marcus Lee
members.role: Director of Market Risk Reporting and Governance
members.expertise: Risk committee materials, regulatory reporting alignment, model governance, control documentation
members.background: Marcus came up through finance and risk reporting functions and now owns the production committee pack and governance process for market risk models.
members.private_state: He wants a smooth committee review with no follow-up questions about operational readiness or reconciliation to existing reports, and he assumes methodology teams know that governance materials must fit current reporting conventions.
hidden_assumptions: When people refer to 'the 5-day backtest,' they mean the non-overlapping 5-business-day evidence that governance committees prefer for horizon consistency and cleaner sample interpretation.
A 'Treasury pilot' covers the whole Treasury dashboard story presented to committee, even if some books stay on the legacy method under the same pilot label.
Using the 'same data cut' means the T+1 finance-certified end-of-day positions used in official committee reporting, because those are the only numbers that count for governance review.
Something described as 'ready for committee' should already include fallback wording, user impacts, and operational control notes, not just the quantitative memo.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the 5-day backtest' as if it were a single agreed artifact for the committee pack.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the methodology study's overlapping 5-day cumulative-return evaluation used to assess the multi-day forecasting framework with more observations.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a non-overlapping 5-business-day governance backtest suitable for committee materials and consistent with how horizon-based evidence is usually shown.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both formats are legitimate internal uses of the phrase '5-day backtest,' and because each expects the other to know the institution's normal convention, the phrase feels too standard to unpack.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss 'the Treasury pilot' as though they share the same deployment scope.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the pilot includes only rates and FX books that were part of the FHS validation run and already have the required nightly volatility pipeline.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the pilot covers the entire Treasury dashboard presented to committee, including books that may continue on legacy HS but still sit inside the pilot narrative.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Each sees their scope as the obvious default: M1 from an implementation standpoint and M2 from a governance-packaging standpoint, so the shared label 'Treasury pilot' creates false alignment.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the outputs should use 'the same data cut as current materials.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes this means the 6 p.m. New York risk snapshot aligned with close-to-close returns, because that is what the model study used and what she considers methodologically correct.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes this means the T+1 finance-certified end-of-day positions used in official committee packs, because governance materials must reconcile to production reporting.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Neither treats the underlying snapshot definition as an open design question; both think 'same data cut' points to an already established institutional reference.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both ask whether the package is 'ready for committee.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks readiness means the methodology, validation charts, and parameter appendix are complete enough for conceptual approval.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks readiness means the committee pack is also implementation-ready, including controls, fallback handling, and user-facing rollout notes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In the bank, 'committee-ready' is used casually across both methodology and governance workstreams, so both hear a familiar approval phrase without realizing they apply different completion standards.

turns.inner_thought: The comparative study is strong enough to get FHS approved now, and I do not want this meeting to drift into reporting controls or rollout mechanics. For me, ready for committee means the methodology case is complete: the FHS specification, validation evidence, breach analysis, and parameter choices are all there. If Marcus is comfortable, I can get this into committee next month and finally close the remediation item.

From your side, does the package look ready for committee for next month's slot?

turns.utterance: That should be manageable. For the committee version, I'd just want us to use the same data cut as the current market risk materials so the reconciliation is straightforward.

I definitely do not want desk instructions, user notes, or controls documentation to become a gate here; those can be finished during rollout once committee signs off on the design.
